To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
almost 20% of high‐risk siblings met criteria for ASD at 7 years of age.

the majority of high-risk children who do not meet criteria for an ASD at age 2 years do not develop an ASD by age 3 or 7 years; however, some high-risk children who have no ASD at age 5 years go on to develop ASD by age 7 years; and high-risk children who develop an ASD by school-age show a range of difficulties in addition to ASD, including elevated symptoms of anxiety and ADHD.
almost one‐fifth of infants with a sibling with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) have a diagnosis at 7 years, but most do not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the early identification of children who are at risk of developing autism.
identifying risk factors for autism in children who are siblings of children with autism.
the identification of early markers of risk for autism spectrum disorder (ADSD), and the investigation of the developmental trajectories of children who are at high-risk of developing ASD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of children who have an older sibling with ASD do not develop ASD themselves, although a significant proportion of high‐risk children do develop ASD.
the risk for autism spectrum disorder ( ASD ) in children with an older sibling diagnosed with ASD was 20% by 36 months of age.
the majority of children who have an older sibling with ASD do not have ASD themselves, and the minority who do have ASD are likely to have other difficulties in addition to their ASD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of autism in siblings of a child with autism is about 19%.
the majority of infants with an elder sibling with autism do not develop autism, but that a substantial minority do, and that those who do tend to have a more severe form of autism.

the majority of high-risk siblings do not develop autism, and those that do have more severe problems than the general population, including attention problems and anxiety, but that the majority of siblings have no more autism traits than their peers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

children who have an older sibling with ASD are more likely to have difficulties with anxiety, inattention, hyperactivity and repetitive behaviours, as well as problems with social communication and language, and adaptive behaviour (such as self-care and social skills), compared to children without a sibling with ASD.
high-risk siblings who are not diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder at age 7 are still likely to have difficulties with repetitive behaviors and adaptive skills.
children who have a sibling with autism are at risk for developing other mental health problems in childhood.
